analysis.one_liner: Makes state and local governments pay damages when their police violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 1992 but never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let people sue the government that employs a police officer — a city, county, or state — when that officer violates their constitutional rights under color of law. It would remove the 'good faith' defense, meaning the government would owe damages even if the officer honestly believed the conduct was lawful. It also set a time limit for such lawsuits, matching the limit already used in existing federal civil-rights suits.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by law enforcement officers gain a new path to compensation. Today, under the Supreme Court's interpretation of the civil-rights statute at 42 U.S.C. 1983, victims can generally sue the individual officer, but local governments can only be held liable if the victim proves the department's own policy or custom caused the harm — a hurdle that defeats most claims. By making the government itself liable without requiring proof of a policy or custom, and by removing the good-faith defense, the bill would shift the burden of officer misconduct from the injured person to the public employer, which has the resources to pay and the power to discipline and train its officers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any state, county, municipality, or other unit of state or local government directly liable in a civil action when its law enforcement officer deprives someone of constitutional or federal rights under color of law [S2] [S3].

Removes the good-faith defense: liability would exist even if the officer had a reasonable, honest belief that the conduct was lawful, so victims would not lose their claim merely because the officer's mistake was understandable [S2] [S3].
Gives lawsuits a clear, existing time limit by adopting the same statute of limitations that already applies to actions under 42 U.S.C. 1983, the federal civil-rights statute [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments — ultimately their taxpayers and insurance funds — would pay damages in cases where an officer violates someone's rights. Police departments would face stronger financial incentives to screen, train, and discipline officers, since the employing government would now be on the hook regardless of whether the individual officer acted in good faith. Cities and counties would likely see higher liability insurance costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes liability without any 'good faith' exception, meaning a government could owe damages even where an officer made a reasonable mistake about what the law required — a standard stricter than the one courts apply to individual officers [S3].

The costs would fall on cities, counties, and states — and through them on taxpayers and municipal liability insurance pools — which would have an incentive to respond with tighter budgets or other offsetting measures rather than absorbing the expense.

The bill creates an additional remedy on top of the existing 42 U.S.C. 1983 action against individual officers, raising the possibility of duplicative litigation and higher legal costs for small local governments [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people injured by police misconduct, the bill addressed a real gap: under current law it is very hard to hold a government department itself accountable, because victims must prove an official policy or custom caused the harm, and individual officers are often shielded by the good-faith defense. The honest cost is that the bill placed that liability on taxpayers-funded local governments without a good-faith exception, which could raise municipal insurance and legal costs everywhere. How those costs balance against stronger deterrence of misconduct was never debated publicly — the bill died in committee without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its civil rights subcommittee, which never held a hearing or markup, so the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Edwards of California introduced the Police Misconduct Civil Remedy Act of 1992 in the House on May 14, 1992 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
On May 20, 1992, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, where no further action was taken [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill expired without a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments and their insurers are better off because the bill died: they never faced direct liability for officer misconduct that bypasses the good-faith defense. People harmed by police misconduct gained nothing; the hurdle of proving a departmental policy or custom remains in place.

for.name: Rep. Don Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it through the House Judiciary Committee, of which he was a senior member.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 20, 1992 and never held a hearing or markup on it, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no partisan split was recorded; it had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of any party [S4].

industries.industry: Municipal liability insurers and local government legal exposure
industries.note: Direct government liability without a good-faith defense would have increased payouts and insurance costs for cities and counties. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran against victims' interest in compensation.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: Departments would face financial consequences for officer misconduct even when individual officers acted in good faith, creating pressure for stricter screening, training, and discipline. Their institutional interest in shielding themselves from damages ran against victims' interest in a remedy.

The bill would have made every unit of state and local government a defendant in civil-rights suits arising from its officers' conduct, a direct fiscal and institutional cost it would naturally resist.
